prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Sometimes, mystified by the behaviorof one of my sons, my wife will point out if it’s age-appropriate, making me wonder why I still shout at ballplayers on tv and argue with the dead. Last week, my oldest son,with a wild pitch, turned my left ankle into an eggplant. I didn’t yell at the doctors who refused my insurance, or get angry with a friend who told me to soak it in bourbon and garlic. No,I read Montaigne who said self-revelation is the purpose of discourse, which, in his day, meant knowing whether to be flattered if a friend didn’t use a food-taster, or amused if a witch cast a spell of weeping on an in-law. Blaise Monluc, the king’s lieutenant general during the civil wars, Montaigne says,threw so many hanged Protestantsdown a well you could reach in and touch the top one’s head. Yes,Monluc, who was fond of saying “When the scaffolds are full, use trees,” knew what was appropriate. On occasion I’ll run into a lobbyto avoid greeting a friend, not because my mind vanishes and I can’t remember his name, which is true, but because I must flee what is darkest in me. In other words, when evicted from a strange lobby into a stranger street, where every scaffold is full and bodies dangle in the long blue sorrow of the afternoon, without context, explanation, or sympathy,it’s good to know, even momentarily, how to live, among the relevant, the passionate, and the confused.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Sometimes, Last, Montaigne

outputs.L1:
Sometimes, mystified by the behavior of one of my sons, my wife will point out that it is age-appropriate, making me wonder why I still shout at ballplayers on TV and argue with the dead. Last week, my oldest son, with a wild pitch, turned my left ankle into an eggplant. I didn’t yell at the doctors who refused my insurance or become angry with a friend who told me to soak it in bourbon and garlic. No, I read Montaigne, who said that self-revelation is the purpose of discourse—which, in his day, meant knowing whether to be flattered if a friend didn’t use a food taster or amused if a witch cast a spell of weeping on an in-law.

Blaise Monluc, the king’s lieutenant general during the civil wars, threw so many hanged Protestants down a well, Montaigne says, that you could reach in and touch the top one’s head. Yes, Monluc, who was fond of saying, “When the scaffolds are full, use trees,” knew what was appropriate.

On occasion, I’ll duck into a lobby to avoid greeting a friend—not because my mind goes blank and I can’t remember his name, which is true, but because I must flee what is darkest in me. In other words, when evicted from a strange lobby onto a stranger street, where every scaffold is full and bodies dangle in the long blue sorrow of the afternoon, without context, explanation, or sympathy, it is good to know, even momentarily, how to live among the relevant, the passionate, and the confused.
outputs.L2: When one of our sons does something that baffles my wife, she sometimes reminds me that his conduct is normal for his age. Her observation leaves me asking why, at mine, I continue to berate athletes on television and quarrel with people who are no longer alive. A week ago, an errant throw from my eldest swelled my left ankle until it resembled an eggplant. Yet I neither shouted at the physicians who would not accept my insurance nor took offense when a friend recommended steeping the injury in bourbon and garlic. Instead, I turned to Montaigne, who believed that conversation exists so we may disclose ourselves. In his time, that might involve deciding whether to feel honored when a friend trusted you enough to skip a food-taster, or entertained when a witch placed a weeping curse on one of your relatives by marriage. Montaigne also writes that Blaise Monluc, the king’s lieutenant general in the civil wars, dropped so many executed Protestants into a well that the uppermost victim’s head could be touched by reaching inside. Monluc—who liked to declare, “When the scaffolds are full, use trees”—certainly understood what suited the occasion. I, meanwhile, sometimes duck into a lobby to escape acknowledging a friend. It is not merely that his name has disappeared from my memory, though it has; I am also running from the most shadowed part of myself. Put another way, when an unfamiliar lobby expels me onto an even less familiar street, beneath an afternoon stretched into blue grief, with every scaffold occupied and corpses hanging everywhere—stripped of context, compassion, and explanation—it helps, if only briefly, to understand how one might exist among those who are pertinent, fervent, and bewildered.
outputs.L3:
The speaker reflects on what constitutes age-appropriate behavior while candidly acknowledging his own irrational habits. Despite his maturity, he still finds himself shouting at ballplayers on television and engaging in imaginary arguments with people who are long dead. These actions suggest that age does not necessarily bring perfect self-control or wisdom; even an older person remains vulnerable to frustration, fantasy, and contradiction.

When his son injures his ankle, however, the speaker does not react with anger or impatience. Instead, the incident leads him toward Montaigne, whose essays examine self-revelation, judgment, and the complexities of human conduct. Montaigne provides a way to think about behavior without reducing it to simple rules. His historical examples show that ideas of what is “appropriate” are often shaped—and sometimes badly distorted—by the surrounding culture. In times marked by cruelty and violence, conduct considered normal or proper may itself be brutal.

The speaker applies this reflective perspective to his own life. He admits that he sometimes avoids his friends, partly because he is forgetful and partly because he wants to escape the darker aspects of his personality. His withdrawal is therefore both an ordinary human failing and an attempt to distance himself from what he fears within himself.

Ultimately, the speaker does not arrive at a clear or permanent code for living. The world remains confusing and sorrowful, and the people in it are passionate, relevant to one another, and deeply bewildered. Yet even a fleeting intuition about how to live among such people has value. A momentary sense of patience, humility, or connection may not solve life’s difficulties, but it can still offer meaningful guidance.
outputs.L4:
At a certain age, one begins to wonder what sort of behavior is still appropriate. Actions that once seemed natural may now appear undignified, while gestures of restraint can feel like mere disguises for fear, fatigue, or wounded pride. I found myself thinking about this after an injury within my family. The accident itself was painful, but the responses surrounding it—the anger, embarrassment, blame, and subsequent avoidance—proved almost as troubling. People who did not know what to say stayed away. Others simplified the event into a story with clear victims and culprits. Memory hardened around those interpretations until each person seemed to possess a different past.

Anger was the most immediate temptation. It offered clarity where there was none, assigning responsibility and turning helplessness into judgment. Yet anger also distorted what it claimed to reveal. Recalled in anger, every careless word became deliberate, every absence became an insult, and every old grievance seemed to predict the present injury. I began to see that memory is not an impartial record. It rearranges experience according to our current passions, preserving certain details while quietly discarding others.

Montaigne understood this instability. His essays return again and again to the difficulty of knowing oneself, much less judging another person. He writes from within uncertainty, observing his habits, fears, contradictions, and bodily frailties without pretending that they form a perfectly consistent character. What makes his self-examination compelling is not the discovery of some pure inner truth, but his willingness to show a mind changing under the pressure of circumstances. He reminds us that behavior cannot be separated from context: age, health, custom, danger, humiliation, and desire all shape what we do.

That insight does not excuse cruelty, but it complicates judgment. History provides countless examples of ordinary people committing or accepting extraordinary violence. Massacres, persecutions, torture, and war are often described as eruptions of barbarism, as if those responsible belonged to a different species. Montaigne’s reflections suggest a less comforting possibility. The impulses behind historical violence—rage, fear, vanity, obedience, resentment, the pleasure of belonging to a righteous group—are not foreign to us. They exist in diminished and socially acceptable forms within everyday life. The distance between domestic hostility and public brutality is enormous, but they may draw upon some of the same human passions.

This recognition makes social avoidance more understandable, though no less painful. People often withdraw from suffering because it threatens the stories they tell about safety, justice, and their own goodness. To approach an injured family is to risk saying the wrong thing, being asked for help, or confronting the fact that misfortune is neither orderly nor deserved. Avoidance can therefore masquerade as tact. Silence can be presented as respect. But beneath these explanations may lie discomfort, cowardice, or the simple wish not to be burdened by another person’s pain.

What, then, is appropriate behavior? There is no rule capable of resolving every case. Age does not automatically produce wisdom, just as youth does not guarantee recklessness. Anger may sometimes defend what deserves defense, but it may also become a shelter from grief. Memory can preserve experience, yet it can also imprison us in a version of events shaped by injury. Even moral judgment, necessary as it is, becomes dangerous when it allows us to imagine that cruelty belongs only to other people.

Montaigne offers no permanent solution. His example is instead one of honest self-revelation: to examine one’s motives without excessive ceremony, to admit inconsistency, and to resist turning private feelings into universal laws. Such honesty does not free us from passion or confusion. It gives us, at best, a momentary orientation—a fleeting guide by which we may live among other people while remembering what people are capable of.

That guidance is fragile, but it may be enough. To acknowledge context without abandoning responsibility, to recognize anger without worshipping it, and to distrust memory without denying the past are modest forms of wisdom. They cannot eliminate humanity’s cruelty or confusion. They can, however, make us less certain of our innocence and more attentive to the suffering of others. In a world governed so often by fear, pride, and violence, that brief clarity may be one of the few reliable forms of hope.
outputs.L5:
### Sometimes, the Last Word

Sometimes we speak because silence feels unfinished. We add explanations, apologies, and conclusions, hoping that the last word will give shape to everything that came before.

Montaigne distrusted such certainty. In his essays, he examined himself without pretending to reach a final answer. His thoughts wandered, contradicted one another, and changed as he changed. “What do I know?” was not a surrender, but an invitation to remain curious.

Perhaps wisdom does not lie in having the last word. Sometimes it lies in recognizing that no word is truly last—that every conclusion may become the beginning of another question.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical, darkly comic prose poem about fatherhood, aging, pain, and moral confusion, weaving together a baseball injury, Montaigne, religious violence, and the awkward avoidance of a friend.
counterfactuals.output:
At forty-eight I tore my rotator cuff throwing batting practice to my son, who watched the ball describe a merciful parabola and then watched me fold beside the pitcher’s mound like a cheap lawn chair.

“Are you dying?” he asked.

“Not today,” I said, which is one of the smaller lies fathers tell.

The doctor showed me the white ghost of my shoulder on a screen and spoke of age as if it were weather moving in from the west. Tendons frayed. Cartilage thinning. A little arthritis setting up its gray furniture. I nodded with the grave attention I usually reserve for restaurant specials, though inside me a choir of medieval penitents had begun striking themselves with belts.

Montaigne says we are all patchwork, all misalignment, and I have loved him for forgiving in advance the crooked cabinet of the self. He wrote about death, stones, thumbs, cannibals, sadness, and the inconvenience of having a body. I read him at night with an ice pack under my shirt while my son slept down the hall, growing by the hour, his bones printing tomorrow without permission.

The world, meanwhile, continued its religious argument with knives.

Men blew up a shrine to prove God was indestructible. Men burned a village to defend the Prince of Peace. Men dragged heaven through the streets by its hair. On television, each side had scripture, smoke, and a spokesman with immaculate cuffs. I changed the channel to baseball and watched a pitcher clutch his elbow after one bad throw.

This seemed honest.

Pain, at least, does not claim divine endorsement. Pain says: here. Pain says: this much. Pain is a bureaucrat with one stamp.

My friend Daniel had written to say his wife was leaving, or had left, or had become a room he could no longer enter. For three weeks I avoided him with the industry of a minor saint. I took different streets. I studied grocery shelves until canned beans acquired philosophical depth. Once I saw him outside the pharmacy and bent to retie a shoe that had no laces.

What could I say? That love is mortal? That marriage is a bad shoulder, held together by habit and inflamed by weather? That Montaigne would have understood? Nothing makes a lonely man lonelier than being handed a French essayist.

My son asked why people kill for God.

I told him people are afraid.

“Of God?”

“Mostly of each other.”

He considered this while winding up to throw. His whole body became intention: knee lifted, glove tucked, bright face briefly severe. I wanted to warn him about torque, zeal, loyalty, the small tearing noises inside every devotion. Instead I crouched behind the plate.

The ball struck the dirt, leapt up, and hit me in the throat.

He ran to me horrified, then laughing, then horrified that he was laughing. This is moral education: two feelings arriving at the same address, each claiming to be the rightful tenant.

I laughed too, though it hurt. Especially because it hurt.

That evening I called Daniel. When he answered, I nearly pretended I had dialed by mistake. We spoke of nothing—the weather, the standings, my shoulder, his leaking faucet. Around the nothing circled the unspeakable, patient as a moon.

Before we hung up, he said, “I knew you were avoiding me.”

“Yes,” I said.

It was not an apology, but it was true, and truth is sometimes the shabby coat mercy wears when all the ceremonial robes are at the cleaners.

My son came in and asked if I would play catch.

I lifted my arm until the pain lit its little chapel.

“Of course,” I said.

Outside, dusk gathered over the yard. He threw badly. I threw worse. Between us the ball kept traveling, white and ridiculous, carrying neither wisdom nor forgiveness, only the ancient dangerous hope that someone would be there to catch it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a surreal personal essay in one dense paragraph that begins with a parent wondering what behavior is age-appropriate and ends with a fleeting insight into how to live amid a confusing, violent world.
counterfactuals.output: I wonder what behavior is age-appropriate, I say to the pediatrician, while my daughter crouches beneath the examination table whispering tax advice to an invisible wolf. The pediatrician, whose white coat is crowded with small blue doors, tells me that childhood is a country with constantly redrawn borders, then opens one of the doors near his heart and releases a moth smelling faintly of antiseptic and rain. Outside, ambulances stitch red thread through the afternoon. On the waiting-room television, buildings collapse without sound, soldiers run through wheat fields, and a man in a suit explains the mathematics of acceptable grief. My daughter emerges holding the wolf by its absent paw and asks whether dead people still get birthdays. I begin an answer about memory, but my mouth fills with aquarium gravel; each word I spit into my palm contains a tiny orange fish. This happens more often now. At breakfast, the spoons accuse me of cowardice. At night, our house lifts several inches from the earth and trembles there, undecided, while sirens comb the streets for someone to blame. I remember being seven and convinced that adults had access to a hidden control room where they adjusted war, weather, hunger, and the price of peaches; now I am the adult, and the control room is a broom closet where a bare bulb swings over unpaid bills. Still, I pack lunches. I cut the crusts into little rafts. I tell my daughter not to hit, not to lie, not to stare at suffering as if it were entertainment, though every screen in the world is teaching the opposite lesson with excellent graphics. On the walk home she skips over cracks that widen behind us into black ravines, and I follow, carrying her coat, her wolf, the fish gasping in my pockets. At the corner, a flock of newspapers rises screaming from a trash can, headlines beating their wings around our faces, and she laughs—not cruelly, but with the astonishment of a body discovering it can make a sound larger than fear. For one second the city becomes transparent: beneath the pavement, roots clasp broken pipes; beneath every uniform, a heart bangs blindly; beneath my own panic, something small keeps setting the table. Then the vision closes, traffic surges, someone far away fires a gun, and my daughter slips her hand into mine, teaching me, before I can name it, that perhaps living here means holding what is warm without pretending the dark is gone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a first-person literary monologue in which an injured father reflects on shouting at televised ballplayers, failed insurance, strange home remedies, Montaigne’s philosophy, Blaise de Monluc’s atrocities, and his own fear of social encounters.
counterfactuals.output:
The doctor says the shoulder will mend crooked if I do not let him operate, and the insurance company says crookedness is not, in itself, a medical emergency. They have a category for everything. A bone may be broken, displaced, shattered, or merely inconvenient. Mine is inconvenient.

So I sit in the blue chair with my arm strapped to my chest and shout at men on television.

“Run, you idiot!”

“Throw it away!”

My daughter looks up from the carpet, where she is arranging plastic horses into families. She has made the black mare the father. I ask why, and she says because it is the largest and saddest.

“You know they can’t hear you,” she tells me.

This is what children think—that uselessness ought to quiet us.

The ballplayers appear enormous on the screen, each grievance magnified: the spit in the grass, the clenched jaw, the accusation made toward heaven. Their bodies obey them even in failure. They leap, collide, rise. When one remains down, six trainers run onto the field. Somewhere, before the replay has finished, a machine has already approved his care.

I despise him for this. Then I despise myself.

My wife has devised treatments. A poultice of grated potato and salt, bound to the shoulder with one of her old scarves. Mustard oil warmed with garlic. A copper bracelet bought from a man at the weekend market who said the metal would draw the pain out through the wrist. Last night she stood behind me and rubbed an egg over my back, whispering words her grandmother taught her. In the morning she cracked it into a glass. A pale thread floated from the yolk like a drowned worm.

“There,” she said. “That’s the injury.”

I wanted to believe her. Belief seems to be another substance the body manufactures less efficiently with age.

The insurance letters are written in a dialect designed to sound like patience. *We understand this may be disappointing.* *You retain the right to appeal.* *Please provide additional documentation.* I have provided the X-ray, the doctor’s report, photographs of the bruise in its yellow, imperial phase. I have described the fall: the ladder shivering beneath me, the gutter coming loose in my hand, the brief, foolish astonishment of the air. Still they ask for proof, as if gravity were an elective procedure.

During the afternoons, when my wife is at work and my daughter is at school, I read Montaigne. I hold the book awkwardly in my good hand. He is always examining himself without seeming vain, as if the self were merely an animal found dead beside the road, worthy of curiosity but not mourning. He writes of pain, fear, habit, idleness, thumbs. He distrusts certainty. “What do I know?” he asks, and the question feels less like surrender than shelter.

I envy the spaciousness of his doubt.

Yet the tower in which he wrote was not far, in history or temperament, from men who had no doubts at all. Blaise de Monluc, soldier, marshal, memoirist: a man from the same century and soil, riding through the religious wars with ropes hanging from his saddle. He wrote of hangings as briskly as another man might record the weather. Villages punished, prisoners executed, terror applied as a tool. He claimed necessity, order, service. The old vocabulary.

I look at the televised crowd, thousands roaring together, and think how quickly a cheer might alter its object.

It comforts me perversely that Montaigne knew men like Monluc existed. His moderation was not innocence. His retreat to books did not mean the world beyond the tower was quiet. Perhaps philosophy is not a cure but a room where brutality must remove its boots before entering.

Still, I wonder what Montaigne would make of my cowardice.

Not the ladder. That was carelessness. I mean the doorbell.

When it rings, my heart begins its senseless drumming. I imagine a neighbor, a parent from school, someone carrying a casserole and a wish to talk. I stay still until they go. Invitations accumulate unanswered. At the supermarket I abandon aisles to avoid acquaintances. If I see another father from my daughter’s class, I study soup labels with an intensity bordering on prayer.

“What are you afraid they’ll do?” my wife asks.

Nothing. That is the horror of it. They will ask how I am, and I will have to select a version. They will mention the weather. I will say, “Yes, terrible,” or “We needed it,” and hear the machinery of myself grinding. They may offer kindness, which is worst of all, because kindness creates a debt no insurer can deny.

On television, the game tightens. A young man misses an easy catch. I am on my feet before I remember the shoulder.

“You useless bastard!” I shout.

Pain flashes white. My daughter flinches.

The room becomes quiet except for the commentators, who are explaining the mistake from three angles.

I sit down. The black mare has fallen on its side. My daughter sets it upright without looking at me.

I want to tell her that shouting is a kind of disguise. That when I condemn the ballplayer, I am condemning the ladder, the claims adjuster, the bone that has not aligned itself, the part of me that hides from harmless people. I am condemning Monluc and borrowing his certainty. I am demanding that bodies behave, that errors be punished, that the world disclose who deserves pain.

Instead I say, “I’m sorry.”

She moves one of the foals nearer the sad father horse.

Montaigne would probably advise me not to make a kingdom of my suffering. He would remind me that pain is sovereign only while it is present, that imagination enlarges both disgrace and dread. But he also admits his fears. That is what I return to: not wisdom, exactly, but candor. He catches himself in contradiction and does not beat the contradiction into submission.

My shoulder throbs beneath the potato poultice. The copper bracelet has turned my wrist green. On the screen, the young man who missed the catch is laughing with a teammate. Already he has escaped the tribunal I built for him.

Tomorrow I will appeal again. I will collect signatures. I will call a stranger and remain on the line while music plays and a recorded voice assures me my suffering is important. Perhaps I will answer the door.

Tonight, I lower the volume.

My daughter brings me the black mare and places it carefully on my knee. I hold it there with my good hand, the largest and saddest of the horses, while the game goes on without my instructions.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem blending mundane domestic comedy with historical brutality. Include a son’s wild pitch, an ankle compared to an eggplant, bourbon and garlic, hanged Protestants, forgotten names, and bodies dangling in a blue afternoon.
counterfactuals.output:
My son’s wild pitch sailed over the fence and cracked the kitchen window, startling the bourbon from my hand and the garlic from the pan, so that for one bright second dinner, baseball, and catastrophe occupied the same small room. He limped in afterward, his ankle already swelling purple as an eggplant, and asked whether ice cream counted as medicine. I said history offers few comforts but yes, sometimes vanilla.

Outside, the blue afternoon went on polishing the roofs. Once, in such weather, hanged Protestants swung above a market square while women compared onions and men pretended not to look. Their names—some written in parish books, some misplaced by rain, some never learned—fell out of memory one by one. Only the bodies remained, dangling in the blue afternoon, terrible punctuation no sentence wished to claim.

I wrapped my son’s ankle in a dish towel. The smoke alarm objected to the garlic. Somewhere a bottle tipped, nobly wasting the bourbon. We laughed because the pan was burning, because the window was broken, because he was alive enough to complain. Behind us stood the forgotten names, patient as furniture, while history, that bad neighbor, kept returning our ball with blood on it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce an experimental paragraph in a wry, associative voice about self-revelation and appropriate behavior, moving fluidly from family life and a sports injury to Renaissance France, personal shame, and an ambiguous conclusion about living among “the relevant, the passionate, and the confused.”
counterfactuals.output: At dinner my mother says honesty is healthy, by which she means I should explain the divorce but not the tattoo, while my brother, excavating peas from the gravy, reminds everyone that I once tore a ligament celebrating a goal I had not, technically, scored. Appropriate behavior is mostly timing. In Renaissance France, I imagine, a minor courtier could confess to envy provided he did so in velvet and attached the confession to a sonnet; shame, properly dressed, was practically a credential. Mine arrives underdressed, carrying old receipts, medical tape, and the memory of limping off the field while both teams politely avoided looking at me. Self-revelation is supposed to open a window, though in my experience it more often sets off an alarm in another room. Still, we tell the family, the physician, the king, the mirror—each according to rank and appetite—what we have done and what we meant to do, then wait for history to distinguish the two. Perhaps this is adulthood: learning which truths require napkins, which require witnesses, and which can only be muttered while taking one’s uncertain place among the relevant, the passionate, and the confused.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
